title: Checkpoint 6: Stockfish (skill 0) vs Magnus
notes: Checkpoint after game 6, from the Queen's Gambit Declined: Magnus plays the yardstick, Stockfish at skill 0. Nothing is studied afterwards.

moves.thought: This is the Orthodox QGD; my pieces need coordination and my king is still in the centre, so before any central break like ...c5 or ...dxc4 I should get castled. 5...0-0 is safe: there are no enemy checks or tempo-gaining captures (6.cxd5 exd5 or 6.Bxf6 Bxf6 are both comfortable), and it prepares ...h6 and ...Nbd7/...c6 next.

Bxc5 is poisoned since d4 recaptures, and Ne4 would plant an unsupported knight that Bxe7/Nxe4 just liquidates, so I challenge the c5 wedge at once with ...b6; after cxb6 I recapture with the c-pawn to keep my pawns linked and open the c-file, and if White supports with b4 I still get bxc5 breaking the chain.

The c5 pawn is a wedge cramping my position, so following my rule about capturing an advanced enemy pawn immediately, 7...bxc5 removes the bind and opens the b-file for my rook; 8.bxc5 c6 with ...Nbd7 and ...a5 gives real counterplay, while 8.dxc5 leaves my strong d5 pawn and the c5 pawn attackable by ...Nbd7. I rejected 7...Bxc5 (simply loses a piece to bxc5 bxc5 dxc5) and 7...Ne4, where my knight would sit on e4 without pawn support per my notebook.

First I checked Bxc5, but d4 simply recaptures and I lose a piece for a pawn, and natural moves like 8...Nbd7 or 8...a5 allow the strong wedge 9.c6! hitting b7/d7 and smothering my queenside, which my rules say to prevent at once. So I block the pawn with 8...c6, fixing White's c5 pawn as a target, taking b5 away from his knight, and keeping my pieces (Bd7/b7, Nbd7, Rb8) ready before any ...e5 break.

Bxc5 is poisoned since d4 recaptures, and ...e5 is premature with my queenside pieces still at home (rule 6), while ...Ne4 puts a knight on a square no pawn can support (rule 9). So I develop with Nbd7, adding pressure to c5 and e5 and preparing the ...e5 break once Bc8 and the rooks are coordinated; I checked that Nxd5 fails because both e6 and c6 guard d5.

The c5 wedge is currently held only by the d4 pawn, so I undermine its base: after 10...e5 11.dxe5 Nxe5 the c5 pawn is defended by nothing and my e7 bishop (plus ...Qc7/...Bd6 support) regains it, while my pieces are all developed and my king is castled so the central break is justified. I checked the captures — Nxd5 cxd5 just loses a knight, and Bxf6 Nxf6 followed by dxe5 still leaves ...Bxc5 or ...Ng4 to win the pawn back.

My e5 pawn is attacked twice (d4 pawn, Nf3) but defended only once (Nd7), so 12.dxe5 Nxe5 13.Nxe5 would simply win a pawn — I must resolve the tension now. Capturing with exd4 keeps material level, leaves a fully symmetric c6/d5 vs c5/d4 structure, and opens the e-file while White's king still sits on e1; I checked the tricks 12.Nxd5 (met by ...Qa5+! 13.Nc3 dxc3 winning material) and 12.Bxf6 Nxf6 13.Nxd5 cxd5 (just drops a piece), so nothing tactical works against it.

I almost played ...Qa5 to hit c3 and c5, but then I counted defenders of e7 and saw Bxe7 just wins a piece, since neither Nd7 nor Rf8 guards it — so every queen move except Qe8 drops the bishop. Taking on c5 also fails to the d4 recapture (knight/bishop for a pawn), so I play Re8, which overprotects e7, puts the rook on the open e-file, and prepares ...Ne4 or ...Nb6/...Bf5 to work against White's weak c5 and d4 pawns.

I first checked the c5 pawn and saw it is over-defended (d4 pawn plus Be3 once d4 vacates), so Nxc5/Bxc5 lose material, and I also spotted that both Nb6 and Bd6 simply drop a piece to cxb6/cxd6. My loosest point is the undefended c6 pawn (Qa4 ideas), so I trade off my problem light-squared bishop with Ba6: after Bxa6 Rxa6 the rook guards both a7 and c6 along the sixth rank and my cramped position eases.

My bishop on a6 was just taken and nothing of mine can recapture (the a7 pawn blocks my rook), so I'm a piece down and need activity; Nxc5 and Bxc5 both lose material since c5 is guarded by d4 and Be3, and b6/d6 squares are poisoned by cxb6/cxd6. Qa5 hits the completely undefended bishop on a6 and also eyes c5, winning a tempo; I verified a2 is guarded by Nc3 so I won't grab it, and White has no checks or tactics against my loose knights after it.

I first checked the tactical traps: the c5 pawn guards b6 and d6 (so Nb6 and Bd6 simply drop a piece to cxb6/cxd6), the Bd3 covers a6 and b5 (Qa6/Qb5 lose the queen), and 15...Ne4 16.Nxe4 dxe4 17.Bxe4 just wins a pawn since my Be7 blocks the e-file, while 15...Ng4 16.Bxh7+! Kxh7 17.Ng5+ Bxg5 18.Bxg5 leaves the g4 knight trapped. So I chose the solid 15...Qc7, which steps off the awkward a5 square, guards the loose c6 pawn (killing the Ne5 ideas), eyes c5 and the b8-h2 diagonal, and prepares ...Nf8-e6 to hit c5/d4; 16.Nb5 cxb5 17.Bxb5 is just a piece sacrifice for me.

Qxh2 is a trap since Rh1 guards h2, and Ne5/Nb6/Bd6/Qd6/Nxc5 all run into pawn captures (dxe5, cxb6, cxd6, dxc5) that cost a piece for a pawn; Ne4 also drops a pawn after Nxe4 dxe4 Bxe4. So I'll reroute the d7-knight via f8 to e6, where it hits both c5 and d4 and keeps everything in my camp defended.

Bxc5 just loses a piece since d4 recaptures and my own c6 pawn blocks the queen from c5, and Qxh2 drops the queen to Rh1, so instead I bring my last piece out with Ne6, pressuring the c5 wedge pawn and d4 while staying defended by f7 and keeping d5 guarded by c6.

I checked ...Nf4 and ...Bxc5/...Nxc5 with full recapture counts: f4 is guarded twice (Be3 and Ne2) against only my queen, so it drops a piece, and the c5/d4 chain holds since the final recapture Rc2xc5 wins my queen. ...Ne4 is the one active square supported by a pawn (d5), so Bxe4 dxe4 is an even trade that relieves my cramp, and my Ne6 can later come to g5 to hold the e4 pawn.

I'm already a piece down (the bishop was lost on a6), so I checked every capture — N6xc5, N4xc5 and Nxd4 all just lose more material after dxc5/Bxc5 recaptures, and Qf4/Qe5/Qg3/Qh2+ all drop the queen to Bxf4, Nxe5, fxg3, Kxh2. Instead of letting Bxe4 trade off my best piece, I play ...f5 so the knight on e4 is permanently supported by both d5 and f5 (rule 9), the b1-h7 diagonal is blocked, and I keep pieces on the board rather than simplifying while behind.

I'm already a piece down, so I must keep tension rather than trade: my key worry is that Ne6 is completely undefended, so White's Ne2-f4 (or Nf3-g5) hits it with tempo, and I checked that ...Nf4 or ...Nxd4/...Nxc5/...Nxf2 all just drop material because Bc1/Rc2/d4 cover those squares. Bf6 clears e7 so Re8 guards the knight, adds a second attacker to d4 alongside Ne6, and keeps my strong f5-supported Ne4 in place without any immediate capture or check against me.

I checked every capture on d4 (Nexd4 and Bxd4) and the recapture chains all end with Ne2/Nf3 collecting a piece for a pawn, and Nxf2+/Ng3+ just drop a knight to Rxf2/fxg3, so there is no tactic here. My knight on e4 is solidly supported by the d5 and f5 pawns, so instead of loosening it I bring my last idle piece into play on the open b-file, keeping c6/d5 guarded and preparing pressure after a White piece lands on b-file squares.

I checked the tempting captures: Nxd4 and Bxd4 fail because d4 is defended twice (Nf3 and Ne2) while my queen can't join the pile-up (c7 doesn't see d4), and Nxg3+/Nxf2+/Bh4/Bg5/Ng5/f4/g5 all lose material (fxg3, Rxf2, Nxh4, Nxg5, gxf4, Nxg5 respectively). With no urgent threat against me — Nh4 hitting f5 is answered by ...Bxh4 — I prefer the solid prophylactic king move, stepping off the a2-g8 diagonal (Bc4 ideas) and keeping my Ne4 doubly supported by d5 and f5 pawns.

White's Bf4 attacks my queen on c7, and f4 is defended twice (g3 pawn and Ne2), so Qxf4 loses the queen; Bxd4 or N6xc5 simply ignore the threat and drop the queen to Bxc7. Nxf4 both removes the attacker and trades my knight for the bishop, and after Nxf4 (or gxf4) my strong Ne4 stays protected by the d5 and f5 pawns while nothing of mine hangs.

My knight on e4 is my best piece and only the f5 pawn supports it, so I want f5 itself permanently guarded — ...g6 does that, blocks White's b1-h7 diagonal, kills any f4-f5 or Nh4 ideas (Bf6 covers h4 and g5), and gives my king luft; the dark-square weakening is harmless since White's dark-squared bishop is already traded. I checked the tactical tries: 24...Ng5 fails to 25.fxg5!, 24...Bxd4 and 24...Qxf4 just drop material to Ne2/Nf3, and 24...Bh4 hangs to Nxh4.

I recounted the e5 knight and saw it is defended twice (d4 and f4 pawns), so Rxe5/Qxe5 and even the undermining ...g5 win nothing and only wreck my king cover; ...Qe7 loses material to Nxc6 forking queen and rook, and ...Nxc5/...Nxf2+/...Ng3+ all just drop the knight to dxc5/Rxf2/fxg3. So I retreat the bishop to g7, keeping my well-supported Ne4 (d5 and f5 guard it), holding the dark squares around my king and keeping c6 defended by the queen.

My knight on e4 is hit twice (f3 pawn and Bd3) but defended only by the d5 pawn, and every active try fails to a recapture count: Nf2+ Rxf2, Ng3+ Nxg3, Ng5 fxg5, Nd6 cxd6, and Nxc5 simply loses to Rxc5 since Qxc5 dxc5 costs the queen. Bxe5 dxe5 also just loses the knight to fxe4 next move, so I retreat to f6 where the knight is defended by my bishop and nothing attacks it.

White's Ne5 is the dominant piece (supported twice by d4 and f4, so Rxe5/Qxe5 just lose material), and it also smothers my Bg7, so I challenge it with ...Nd7, which is safely guarded by my queen — Nxd7 Qxd7 removes the blockader and opens the long diagonal onto d4. I rejected ...g5 because it opens my king (rule 10) and ...Ne4 because Bxe4 fxe4 fxe4 dxe4 leaves me an unsupported passer while the knight stays on e5.

The e5 knight is White's best piece while my g7 bishop is permanently blocked by the d4/f4/c5 dark-square pawns, so trading bad bishop for strong knight is the right simplification; e5 is defended twice by pawns so the exchange is materially even (B for N, no loss). Compared with ...Nxe5, after Bxe5 dxe5 I still keep a knight that can hop to f6/b6 to defend the backward d5 pawn on the opening d-file, whereas ...Nxe5 dxe5 would leave me with only a dead bishop to hold d5.

I checked the e5 pawn and saw it is guarded by the f4 pawn, so Nxe5/Rxe5/Qxe5 all just lose material, and Nxc5 fails to Rxc5 because my queen's recapture is blocked by my own c6 pawn (nothing else covers c5). With White's queen boxed in on d1 (c2 and d3 blocked) there is no immediate threat, so I regroup the knight via f8 toward e6, where it will blockade, cover e6 against e5-e6, and hit c5 and f4.

I rejected 30...g5 because after 31.Bxf5 my f-pawn loses its g6 defender, and Qxe5/Rxe5/Rxb3 all lose material to fxe5 or axb3 (rule 2). Instead 30...Ne6 activates my worst piece, blockades the e6 square so White's e5 wedge can never advance with Bxf5 tricks, and pressures f4 and c5 while eyeing the fork square d4 (31.Nd4? Nxd4 hits c2 and f3 with no recapture).

I first checked the tempting activity: Qb6 and Qd6 lose the queen to cxb6/cxd6, Nxf4 and Nxc5 just drop a piece since Qc1 guards f4 and Rc2/Nb3 hold c5, and Qxe5 fails to fxe5 — so no capture works. The c-file is blocked by White's own c5 pawn, so White's only real plan is piling on the g-file against g6, and pushing ...g5 would open lines to my king against Bd3 and Qc1 (rule 10). So I play the safe prophylactic Kg7, guarding g6, freeing h8 for a rook, and keeping every piece defended.

I first counted defenders on every capture and rejected them all: Nxf4 and Nxc5 both drop a piece (Qc1 covers f4 via c1-d2-e3 and c5 down the file), Nd4/...d4 lose to Nxb3's coverage of d4, Rb5 loses to Bxb5, and a5 loses to Nxa5 — the knight on b3 and queen on c1 blanket a5/c5/d4/f4. Rb4 is the one active move that no White unit attacks right now, it hits the b3 knight and, crucially, creates the real threat ...Nxf4 Qxf4 Rxf4 (nothing recaptures on f4 because White's own f3 pawn blocks Rf2), forcing White to spend time with a3 or Qc3.

Every capture fails on recount (Rxb3 axb3, Nxc5 Nxc5 and Qxc5 Qxc5, Nxf4/Rxf4 Rxf4, Qxe5 Rxe5), so I looked for a constructive move: 33...d4 creates a protected passer defended twice (Ne6 and Rb4) while attacked only by Nb3, and it also denies White's knight the d4 square and keeps Bd3 entombed — Bc4 or Bb5 trying to hit it just drops the bishop to Rxb4-file/rank coverage.

I first verified that d4 is attacked twice (Nb3, Rd1) but defended twice (Rb4, Ne6), so 35.Nxd4 Nxd4 36.Rxd4 Rxd4 just loses material for White; I also rejected Qa5 (Nxa5!), Nxf4 (Qc1 covers f4) and Qxe5 (fxe5) after counting captures. Ra4 keeps the rook on the fourth rank still guarding d4, dodges the a3 tempo-gaining push, and attacks the completely undefended a2 pawn (Qc1 and Rd1 don't cover it), while b5 stays poisoned for the bishop because my c6 pawn guards it.

My d4 pawn is attacked three times (Nb3, c5, e5) and only defended once by Ra4, so it cannot be held — and every other rook retreat drops material (cxb4 after Rb4, Qxa3, Bxc4, Nxa5). So I grab the loose a2 pawn with Rxa2, which is attacked by nothing, lands actively on the second rank hitting Rg2, and if White tries Qc2 then Rxc2 Rxc2 wins the queen for a rook.

My rook on a2 is hanging to Rg2 (defended only by Kh1), but White's knight on d4 is completely undefended — Rd1 is blocked by its own bishop and the queen on c1 doesn't cover d4 — so 36...Nxd4 at once just loses a rook to Rxa2. By trading first with Rxg2, after Kxg2 I can take the knight with ...Nxd4 and restore material equality (Q+R+N vs Q+R+B, five pawns each), since White has no check or counter-threat after Rxg2 (Nxe6+ or Nxf5+ simply drop a piece for nothing).

My rook on g2 is undefended and attacked by Kh1, and almost every active square fails (Ra2 Bxa2, Rb2/Rc2/Re2/Rd2 drop it, Rg3 is trapped by 38.Kg2, Rf2 by 38.Kg1, Rg4 hxg4, Rg5 fxg5), so the only genuinely safe square is g8. After 37...Rg8 my e8 rook still guards e6, so White can only liquidate with Bxe6 Rxe6 Nxe6+ Qxe6, leaving a balanced Q+R ending where my queenside majority and outside a-pawn give me the better chances; if White delays, ...Nxd4 keeps me up the exchange.

I'm in check from the knight on e6 and it also hits my queen on c7, so the queen is lost whichever way I step; I therefore picked the king move that keeps my pieces least loose — Kf7 attacks the e6 knight and, crucially, my king blocks the c4-g8 diagonal so the rook on g8 isn't also hanging to the bishop (after Nxc7+ Kg7 the g8 rook stays guarded and ...Rc8 can hunt the loose knight on c7). Kh6 or Kh8 would leave both rooks loose (Kxg2 and Bxg8 at once), losing even more material.

The check is a discovered one from Bc4 along the a2-g8 diagonal, so my king must leave that diagonal while still guarding the loose rook on g8 — Ke7 loses it outright to Bxg8. Between Kf8 and Kg7 both keep g8 defended, but Kf8 invites Rd8+ with tempo on the back rank, so I prefer Kg7, where my king stays active, shields g6/h7 and only faces checks that cost me nothing extra.

I'm down a queen, bishop and knight for a rook, so my only job is to avoid losing more material or getting mated: Kf8 walks into Ne6+ followed by Rd8+ Rxd8 Nxd8, trading off one of my last rooks, and Kh6 exposes my king to g4/Rd6 and Rxh7+ ideas. Kh8 keeps the g8 rook defended by the king, gives White no check and no capture (Bd5 is met by cxd5, Rd8 by Rxd8), so I tuck the king in the corner.

I'm far behind in material, so my priority is removing White's mating threats: my h7 pawn is loose to Rxh7+ and the g-file is drafty, while pushing ...g5 or ...h5 would open my king to the queen and f4 pawn exactly as my notebook warns. Rg7 defends h7, blocks the seventh rank, and offers a rook trade that strips an attacker from the attack.
Only one legal move exists — Rg8 is forced to answer the check on d8.
